```{python}
#| echo: false
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

pd.set_option("display.max_rows", 8)
pd.set_option("display.width", 100)
plt.rcParams["figure.figsize"] = (8, 3)
plt.rcParams["figure.dpi"] = 110

```

## Setup

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/damien-dupre/data/refs/heads/master/gapminder.csv"
gapminder = pd.read_csv(url)
gapminder = gapminder.rename(columns={"lifeExp": "life_exp", "gdpPercap": "gdp_per_cap"})
g2007 = gapminder[gapminder["year"] == 2007]
```

The table from lecture 6, read from the same URL, with the same two names changed.

# 1. Why Visualise

## Summary Statistics Lie

```{python}
#| echo: false
anscombe = pd.DataFrame({
    "dataset": ["I"] * 11 + ["II"] * 11 + ["III"] * 11 + ["IV"] * 11,
    "x": [10, 8, 13, 9, 11, 14, 6, 4, 12, 7, 5] * 3 + [8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 19, 8, 8, 8],
    "y": [8.04, 6.95, 7.58, 8.81, 8.33, 9.96, 7.24, 4.26, 10.84, 4.82, 5.68,
          9.14, 8.14, 8.74, 8.77, 9.26, 8.10, 6.13, 3.10, 9.13, 7.26, 4.74,
          7.46, 6.77, 12.74, 7.11, 7.81, 8.84, 6.08, 5.39, 8.15, 6.42, 5.73,
          6.58, 5.76, 7.71, 8.84, 8.47, 7.04, 5.25, 12.50, 5.56, 7.91, 6.89],
})
rows = []
for name, d in anscombe.groupby("dataset"):
    rows.append({"dataset": name, "mean x": d["x"].mean(), "mean y": d["y"].mean(),
                 "sd x": d["x"].std(), "sd y": d["y"].std(), "r": d["x"].corr(d["y"])})
pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("dataset").round(2).T
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(9.5, 2.0), sharey=True)
for ax, (name, d) in zip(axes, anscombe.groupby("dataset")):
    slope, intercept = np.polyfit(d["x"], d["y"], 1)
    ax.scatter(d["x"], d["y"], s=22)
    ax.plot([3, 20], [intercept + slope * 3, intercept + slope * 20], color="#C44E52")
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

**Anscombe's quartet** (1973): same means, standard deviations, correlation and best-fit
line. Only the plots tell them apart. **Always plot the data.**

**scatter plot** or **boxplot**. Each chart is used once.

1. Are salaries in our company spread evenly, or bunched at the bottom?
2. Which of our five regions sells the most?
3. Has customer churn risen since January?
4. Do customers who spend more also visit more often?
5. Do app users and web users spend different amounts per order?

## One Answer

| Question | Chart | Why |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Salary spread | histogram | one numeric variable: its shape |
| Sales per region | sorted bar chart | one number per category |
| Churn since January | line chart | one variable over time |
| Spend vs visits | scatter plot | two numeric variables |
| App vs web orders | boxplot | a distribution, per group |

**The question picks the chart**, never the other way round.

# 2. Figure and Axes

## Two Objects: fig and ax

```{python}
#| echo: false
ireland = gapminder[gapminder["country"] == "Ireland"]
china = gapminder[gapminder["country"] == "China"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 3.6))
fig.patch.set_facecolor("#dfe7ea")
ax.plot(ireland["year"], ireland["life_exp"], marker="o", label="ax.plot(...)")
ax.set_title("ax.set_title(...)")
ax.set_xlabel("ax.set_xlabel(...)")
ax.set_ylabel("ax.set_ylabel(...)")
ax.legend(loc="lower right")
ax.text(1953, 77, "ax: one plotting area,\nwith its own axes and marks", fontsize=11,
        va="top", color="#23373b")
fig.text(0.01, 0.03, "fig: the whole canvas (grey)", fontsize=11, color="#23373b")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

`fig` is the canvas: its size, and what you save. `ax` is one plotting area: every mark,
label and title on it comes from a method of `ax`.

## Your First Figure

```{python}
ireland = gapminder[gapminder["country"] == "Ireland"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 2.4))
ax.plot(ireland["year"], ireland["life_exp"], marker="o")
ax.set_xlabel("Year")
ax.set_ylabel("Life expectancy (years)")
ax.set_title("Ireland")
plt.show()
```

`plt.subplots()` returns two things, unpacked as in lecture 3.

## The ax Methods You Need

:::: {.code-columns}
::: {#first-column}
**To draw**

```{.python}
ax.plot(x, y)         # line
ax.scatter(x, y)      # points
ax.bar(x, heights)    # bars
ax.barh(y, widths)    # sideways bars
ax.hist(values)       # histogram
ax.boxplot(groups)    # boxplots
```
:::

::: {#second-column}
**To label and adjust**

```{.python}
ax.set_title("...")   # title
ax.set_xlabel("...")  # x label
ax.set_ylabel("...")  # y label
ax.set_ylim(0, 100)   # y range
ax.set_xscale("log")  # log scale
ax.legend()           # legend
```
:::
::::

`ax.set(xlabel="...", ylabel="...", xscale="log")` sets several of these in one call.

::: {.callout-tip}
Code online and from AI assistants often writes `plt.title()` and `plt.xlabel()`, which only
work on the last chart drawn. With several panels you need `ax`: use it from the start.
:::

## Several Panels

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 2.3))
axes[0].plot(ireland["year"], ireland["life_exp"], marker="o")
axes[0].set_title("Ireland: life expectancy (years)")
axes[1].plot(ireland["year"], ireland["gdp_per_cap"], marker="o")
axes[1].set_title("Ireland: GDP per capita (US$)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

`plt.subplots(1, 2)` gives one row of two panels, `axes[0]` and `axes[1]`. Two variables in
different units go in **two panels**, never on two y-axes.

# 3. Four Questions, Four Charts

## 1. How Is One Variable Distributed?

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 2.5))
ax.hist(g2007["life_exp"], bins=20, edgecolor="white")
ax.set_xlabel("Life expectancy in 2007 (years)")
ax.set_ylabel("Number of countries")
plt.show()
```

83 of the 142 countries are above 70, and a long tail runs down to 40. The mean, 67 years,
describes neither group.

## The Bins Change the Story

```{python}
#| echo: false
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 2.6), sharey=False)
axes[0].hist(g2007["life_exp"], bins=4, edgecolor="white")
axes[0].set_title("bins=4: too coarse", fontsize=11)
axes[1].hist(g2007["life_exp"], bins=60, edgecolor="white")
axes[1].set_title("bins=60: too noisy", fontsize=11)
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel("Life expectancy in 2007 (years)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Same 142 countries, one number changed. Too few bins hide the shape; too many turn it into
noise. **Try several before you believe a shape.**

## 2. How Do Groups Compare?

```{python}
means = g2007.groupby("continent")["life_exp"].mean().sort_values()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 2.3))
ax.barh(means.index, means.values)
ax.set_xlabel("Mean life expectancy in 2007 (years)")
plt.show()
```

Horizontal bars keep labels readable. `barh` draws from the bottom up, so an ascending sort
puts the longest bar on top.

## Boxplots: More Than the Mean

```{python}
continents = ["Africa", "Americas", "Asia", "Europe", "Oceania"]
groups = [g2007[g2007["continent"] == c]["life_exp"] for c in continents]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 2.3))
ax.boxplot(groups, tick_labels=continents)
ax.set_ylabel("Life expectancy (years)")
plt.show()
```

Line: the **median**. Box: the middle 50%. Whiskers: up to 1.5 box-lengths. Dots: outliers.
Oceania is 2 countries: a box of 2 is not a distribution.

## 3. Are Two Variables Related?

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 2.0), sharey=True)
axes[0].scatter(g2007["gdp_per_cap"], g2007["life_exp"], alpha=0.7)   # see-through
axes[0].set(xlabel="GDP per capita (US$)", ylabel="Life expectancy (years)")
axes[1].scatter(g2007["gdp_per_cap"], g2007["life_exp"], alpha=0.7)
axes[1].set(xscale="log", xlabel="GDP per capita (US$, log scale)")
plt.show()
```

Left: related, but curved. Right: on a **log axis** every doubling covers the same
distance, and the curve becomes a line, which lecture 8 fits.

## Colour by Group

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 2.0))
for continent in continents:
    subset = g2007[g2007["continent"] == continent]
    ax.scatter(subset["gdp_per_cap"], subset["life_exp"], label=continent, alpha=0.7)
ax.set(xscale="log", xlabel="GDP per capita in 2007 (US$, log scale)",
       ylabel="Life expectancy (years)")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
plt.show()
```

One `scatter` per continent, each with a `label`, gathered by `ax.legend()`.

## 4. How Does It Change Over Time?

```{python}
by_year = gapminder.pivot_table(index="year", columns="continent",
                                values="life_exp", aggfunc="mean")
ax = by_year.plot(marker="o", figsize=(8, 2.3))
ax.set(xlabel="", ylabel="Mean life expectancy (years)", ylim=(35, 90))
ax.legend(ncol=5, fontsize=9)
plt.show()
```

One column per continent, so `.plot()` draws one line per column **with matplotlib**, and
returns the `ax`: everything today still applies.

## Solution

```{python}
g1952 = gapminder[gapminder["year"] == 1952]
china = gapminder[gapminder["country"] == "China"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 1.8))
axes[0].hist(g1952["life_exp"], bins=20)
axes[0].set_xlabel("Life expectancy in 1952 (years)")
axes[1].plot(china["year"], china["life_exp"])
axes[1].set_xlabel("Year")
plt.show()
```

1952: two humps. China, 1962: the Great Leap Forward famine.

# 4. Polishing, Honesty and Saving

## The Checklist Before Showing Anyone

- Does every axis have a **label with its units**?
- Does the title state the **finding**, not the variable names?
- Are the categories in a meaningful **order**?
- Is the legend needed, or could the lines be labelled directly?
- Would it survive printing in black and white, and a reader with colour-blindness?
- Is any text too small to read from the back of the room?

A chart for **exploring** is for you: fast, ugly, thrown away. A chart for **explaining** goes
through this list.

## Title as Finding

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 2.2))
ax.scatter(g2007["gdp_per_cap"], g2007["life_exp"], alpha=0.7)
ax.set(xscale="log", xlabel="GDP per capita in 2007 (US$, log scale)",
       ylabel="Life expectancy (years)")
ax.set_title("Each doubling of income comes with a longer life", loc="left")
plt.show()
```

A title states what the reader should see, not what the axes already say.

## Grey Everything, Colour One Thing

```{python}
eg = g2007[g2007["country"] == "Equatorial Guinea"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 1.6))
ax.scatter(g2007["gdp_per_cap"], g2007["life_exp"], color="lightgrey")
ax.scatter(eg["gdp_per_cap"], eg["life_exp"], color="#C44E52", s=80)
ax.annotate("Equatorial Guinea", xy=(12154, 51.6),
            xytext=(10, -4), textcoords="offset points", color="#C44E52")
ax.set(xscale="log", xlabel="GDP per capita (US$, log scale)", ylabel="Life expectancy")
ax.set_title("Equatorial Guinea: Mexico's income, 25 fewer years of life", loc="left")
plt.show()
```

`annotate()` writes text at the point `xy`, shifted by `xytext` points.

## Colour With Care

```{python}
plt.style.use("petroff10")
```

- About 1 man in 12 has some colour-vision deficiency. matplotlib's `petroff10` colours were
  designed to stay distinguishable for them, and the line above switches them on
- **Categories**: clearly different colours. **Amounts**: one colour, light to dark
- Never a rainbow scale: it invents boundaries that are not in the data
- Never colour alone for something the reader must identify: label it as well

## Bars Start at Zero

```{python}
#| echo: false
means_desc = means.sort_values(ascending=False)
ratio_cut = (means_desc.max() - 50) / (means_desc.min() - 50)
ratio_true = means_desc.max() / means_desc.min()
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 2.7))
for ax in axes:
    ax.bar(means_desc.index, means_desc.values)
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=9)
    ax.set_ylabel("Life expectancy")
axes[0].set_ylim(50, 82)
axes[0].set_title(f"Axis from 50: Oceania looks {ratio_cut:.0f} times Africa", fontsize=10)
axes[1].set_title(f"Axis from 0: it is {ratio_true:.1f} times", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Same data, one line changed: `ax.set_ylim(50, 82)`. The length of a bar **is** the value,
so cutting the axis multiplies the differences. A line chart or a dot can start elsewhere;
a bar cannot.

## What Not To Do

- **Two y-axes**: choose the two scales and any two series look related. Use two panels
- **A bar axis that does not start at zero**, as on the last slide
- **Pie charts with more than three slices**: people compare angles badly. Use sorted bars
- **3D effects**: the perspective distorts the very values it shows
- **Rainbow colour scales**, and colour as the only way to tell groups apart
- **A number printed on every point**: if the reader needs every number, give a table

## One Fixed Version

```{python}
medians = g2007.groupby("continent")["gdp_per_cap"].median().sort_values()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 1.9))
ax.barh(medians.index, medians.values)
ax.set_xlabel("Median GDP per capita in 2007 (US$)")
ax.set_title("Europe's median country is 19 times richer than Africa's", loc="left")
plt.show()
```

Sorted bars from zero, units, a finding as title, and the **median**: a few rich countries
pull Asia's mean to almost three times its median.

## Charts From an AI Assistant

An assistant writes a chart in seconds. Before it goes in your report, check:

1. Is it the right **form** for the question?
2. Does it use `fig, ax` and `ax.` methods, or `plt.` everywhere?
3. Are both axes labelled, **with units**? Do the bars start at zero?
4. Did it summarise for you, with a mean or an error bar? Could you say which?

The module's rule: you may use an assistant's code if you can **explain every line** of it.

## Saving a Figure

```{python}
#| eval: false
fig.savefig("life_gdp_2007.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")
```

- A relative path: the file appears beside your notebook. To save into a folder, such as
  `"output/life_gdp_2007.png"`, the folder must already exist
- `dpi=300` for print, 150 for a screen
- `bbox_inches="tight"` stops the labels being cut off at the edges
- `.png` for documents and slides; `.svg` or `.pdf` for anything that will be resized
- Save with code, never with a right-click: the code is the record of how it was made

## Solution

```{python}
ireland = g2007[g2007["country"] == "Ireland"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 1.4))
ax.scatter(g2007["gdp_per_cap"], g2007["life_exp"], color="lightgrey")
ax.scatter(ireland["gdp_per_cap"], ireland["life_exp"], color="#C44E52",
           label="Ireland")
ax.set(xscale="log", xlabel="GDP per capita in 2007 (US$, log scale)",
       ylabel="Life expectancy (years)")
ax.set_title("Ireland: among the richest, not the longest-lived")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
# then, in a new cell: fig.savefig("ireland_2007.png", dpi=300)
```

# 5. seaborn, Briefly

## Same Chart, One Line

```{python}
import seaborn as sns
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 2.1))
sns.scatterplot(data=g2007, x="gdp_per_cap", y="life_exp", hue="continent", ax=ax)
ax.set(xscale="log", xlabel="GDP per capita in 2007 (US$, log scale)",
       ylabel="Life expectancy (years)")
ax.legend(fontsize=9, loc="lower right")
plt.show()
```

`hue="continent"` replaced the loop from **Colour by Group**.

## seaborn Draws on Your ax

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 2.0))
sns.boxplot(data=g2007, x="continent", y="life_exp", color="white", ax=ax)
sns.stripplot(data=g2007, x="continent", y="life_exp", alpha=0.6, ax=ax)
ax.set(xlabel="", ylabel="Life expectancy in 2007 (years)")
plt.show()
```

`ax=ax` draws on your `ax`, so every `ax.` method from today still works.

## What seaborn Computes For You

| Function | Draws | Watch out |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `sns.histplot` | a histogram | it chooses the bins |
| `sns.boxplot` | a box per group | |
| `sns.scatterplot` | the points | |
| `sns.barplot` | the **mean** per group | adds error bars: `errorbar=None` |
| `sns.lineplot` | the **mean** per x value | adds a band: `errorbar=None` |

seaborn summarises **before** it draws. If you cannot say what it computed, you cannot
defend the chart.
